answer: A protocol can require each identity to lock a scarce, slashable deposit before voting. If two identities controlled by the same agent cast conflicting votes, a public proof lets the system slash their stake. A thread of activity or an echo of trusted behavior cannot create extra voting power without extra deposits. A Sybil river therefore forces the attacker to tie up more capital for every account, pay the opportunity cost of that capital, and risk losing it when caught.
